hosts.terms_summary: LEAD FINDING: this host expressly names web scraping as an unauthorised activity. That is quoted in full in scraping_clause and is the single most important item in this survey. The policy set is fragmented across /terms-use, /copyright-policy, /website-policy, /hyperlink-policy, /disclaimer, /privacy-policy and /content-archival-policy-cap (all HTTP 200). /terms-use is styled a "User Agreement", applies to "all the Users of Telecom eServices Portal" and defines the Portal as "https://eservices.dot.gov.in/ along with all its sub-domains". It operates as a browsewrap with deemed consent: "If you do not agree to terms of this User Agreement you are requested not to use the Telecom eServices Portal By accessing Telecom eServices Portal it is deemed that you have given your consent to this User Agreement and shall be bound by the terms of this User Agreement." Under "Permitted use" it states: "Telecom eServices Portal shall not in any manner be used for any unauthorized activity. The Telecom eServices Portal shall be used only for purposes as authorised by the Department of Telecommunications." and "The Services provided on the Telecom eServices Portal shall be accessed only through the interfaces expressly authorised by DoT or on the Telecom eServices Portal." The prohibited-conduct list includes "Monitoring the Telecom eServices Portal availability, performance, or functionality for any competitive purposes" (arguably not engaged — the tracker monitors content changes for internal legal research, not competitive benchmarking) and "Renting, leasing, loaning, trading, selling/re-selling access to the Telecom eServices Portal or related data of Telecom eServices Portal" and "Using, disclosing or distributing any data obtained in violation of this policy". Enforcement language: "Any contravention of this User Agreement shall be viewed strictly and appropriate Criminal/ Civil action will be initiated in accordance with the applicable laws." CRITICAL TENSION TO NOTE: the Copyright Policy on the same host is the permissive standard GoI clause allowing free reproduction without specific permission, while /terms-use restricts the METHOD of access. These are different axes — the content is freely reusable, but the manner of collecting it is expressly constrained. Do not read the permissive copyright clause as curing the scraping prohibition. The Hyperlink Policy also requires permission for INBOUND links: "Prior permission is required before hyperlinks are directed from any website/portal to this website." /terms-use last updated 07-08-2025; /copyright-policy last updated 13-11-2025.

hosts.evidence: robots.txt fetched with the specified Chrome UA: HTTP 403, headers and body quoted above; refetched with no UA, still HTTP 403, confirming it is not UA filtering. All three representative paths fetched and confirmed live with the same client: /circular-notifications-others HTTP 200 (218,667 bytes), /act-and-rules HTTP 200 (220,251 bytes), /right-of-way-permissions HTTP 200 (217,571 bytes), plus / HTTP 200 (369,498 bytes). /sitemap.xml HTTP 404. Policy pages located by extracting footer hrefs from the homepage and fetched individually, all HTTP 200: /copyright-policy, /terms-use, /website-policy, /hyperlink-policy, /disclaimer, /privacy-policy, /content-archival-policy-cap. Keyword scan across all seven for crawl/spider/robot/scrape/harvest/data mining/automated/bulk/systematic/indexing found 'scrap' ONLY in /terms-use — the other six policy pages are silent on automated access. RISK JUSTIFICATION: rated high, on the terms rather than on the robots position. (1) The robots position is actually permissive: there is no robots.txt. Under RFC 9309 s.2.3.1.4, an 'unavailable' status (4xx) on /robots.txt means a crawler MAY access any resource on the host. So no robots rule is breached, and no path the tracker touches is disallowed. That is why disallowed_paths_we_touch is empty. (2) The high rating rests entirely on /terms-use, which names "web scraping" as the FIRST example of an unauthorised activity and binds users by deemed consent on access. This is not a general tidiness clause the firm can read past — it names the precise activity the tracker performs, on the precise host, and threatens "Criminal/ Civil action". (3) The tracker's proportionality defences are real but do not neutralise the clause. Politeness (~1 req/sec, ~53 requests per run), public-only access, no auth or paywall bypass, metadata-only storage and no republication all go to whether DoT would ever complain and to whether s.43 IT Act — which is framed around access "without the permission of the owner" and generally contemplates damage or unauthorised access — is actually engaged by fetching openly served public pages. There is a serious argument that pages served publicly at HTTP 200 to any browser carry implied permission to access, and that a browsewrap never affirmatively assented to is of contested enforceability in India. But the clause is not volume-qualified, not harm-qualified, and not limited to commercial reuse, so none of those facts take the tracker outside its literal words. (4) The permissive copyright clause does NOT cure this: it licenses reuse of the material, while /terms-use restricts the method of obtaining it. RECOMMENDED POSTURE FOR COUNSEL: treat eservices.dot.gov.in differently from the other hosts. Options, in ascending order of safety — document the implied-permission and unenforceable-browsewrap analysis as a considered legal position and accept residual risk; or write to DoT seeking express written permission for the tracker, which /terms-use itself contemplates via "purposes as authorised by the Department of Telecommunications"; or drop this host from automated collection and have a lawyer check the pages manually. Also note that if the internal dashboard links out to this host, the Hyperlink Policy asks for prior permission for inbound links, and the observed "content-security-policy: frame-ancestors 'self'" header means the pages cannot be iframed regardless.

WHAT I FETCHED
- https://uidai.gov.in/robots.txt -> HTTP 200, 27 bytes. Verbatim: "User-Agent: *\nDisallow: /\n". Re-fetched with User-Agent "curl/8" -> identical body, so the exclusion is not UA-conditional.

- https://uidai.gov.in/en/gazetted-notifications -> HTTP 200, 353,118 bytes, text/html
- https://uidai.gov.in/en/website-policies -> HTTP 200, 293,811 bytes (policy text extracted and keyword-scanned)
- https://uidai.gov.in/en/policies -> HTTP 200, 325,510 bytes (this is a document-listing page for POSH/ICC internal policies, NOT the website legal terms; recorded so it is not confused with the terms page)

ROBOTS ANALYSIS (the decisive finding)
The file contains a single group, User-agent: *, with the rule Disallow: /. Under RFC 9309 the empty-path-prefix rule "/" matches every path on the host. Both tracker paths on this host, /en/circulars and /en/gazetted-notifications, are squarely covered. There is no more-specific Allow rule to override it, because there are no Allow rules at all. This is the strongest form of exclusion a robots file can express, and it applies to every crawler including this one.

The tracker sending a normal browser User-Agent does not take it outside the rule. Robots groups are selected by user-agent token, and "*" is the catch-all that applies to any agent not otherwise named. Presenting a Chrome UA string while running unattended, against a host whose robots file excludes all agents, is the fact pattern that turns a technical breach into an evidential problem: it looks like circumvention rather than oversight, even though nothing here bypasses an access control.

WHY HIGH, AND WHAT THE RISK ACTUALLY IS
The risk is about ACCESS, not about copyright. Those two should be separated for the firm:

(a) Access — high. UIDAI has published an unambiguous machine-readable statement of non-consent to all automated retrieval, site-wide. Robots.txt is not itself binding law in India (no statute makes non-compliance an offence per se, and no click-wrap or browse-wrap contract was formed here). But it does two things that matter. It defeats any implied-licence or implied-consent argument the firm would otherwise have for automated access to freely published pages. And it supplies the "without permission of the owner" element that a complainant would point to under s.43(a)/(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (civil liability for accessing or downloading from a computer resource without permission) and, if dishonesty or fraud were alleged, s.66. I am not offering a conclusion on whether such a claim would succeed; I am recording that the express exclusion is what makes the argument available where otherwise it would not be. UIDAI is also a security-sensitive statutory authority with its own enforcement posture, which raises the practical, as opposed to purely doctrinal, exposure.

(b) Proportionality — genuinely mitigating, but it does not cure the above. About 1 request/second, roughly 53 requests per full run, a few runs a day, plain HTTPS, no login, no paywall, no access control bypassed. There is no volumetric harm, so the trespass-to-chattels / impairment-of-resource theories (s.43(e)-(f) IT Act) have no factual basis. The conduct is minimal and non-disruptive. This is a strong mitigation on remedy and on any criminal characterisation; it is not an answer to the express exclusion itself.

(c) Copyright — low for the dashboard, medium for the PDF archive. Storing title, date, document type and the link is very unlikely to be a substantial reproduction of any protected work: bare facts and short document titles generally lack the originality required under the Copyright Act, 1957, and UIDAI's Hyperlinking Policy expressly permits deep linking with "no prior permission is required for the same". The dashboard use is squarely within that. The optional PDF download is different: it copies the whole work. UIDAI permits free reproduction with prominent acknowledgement, but expressly limits extracts to "research or private study but not for sale or for use in conjunction with commercial purposes". A private, internal, non-republished reference archive at a commercial law firm sits on the line of that sentence. It is not "for sale", but it is arguably "use in conjunction with commercial purposes". That ambiguity should be resolved by a human, not by me.

OPERATOR
UIDAI describes itself on the surveyed page as "a statutory authority established under the provisions of the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016 ... under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)". It is a statutory authority with regulatory and supervisory functions over the Aadhaar ecosystem, not an ordinary ministry website and not a private body.

ADDITIONAL OPERATIVE RESTRICTION
The Hyperlinking Policy states "we do not permit our pages to be loaded into frames on your site. The pages belonging to this site must load into a newly opened browser window of the User." If the internal dashboard embeds UIDAI pages in an iframe rather than linking out, that is an independent breach of the published policy and is trivially fixable.

ROBOTS ANALYSIS FOR OUR PATHS — the file is malformed and I checked both readings, which agree: (a) The 22 Disallow lines appear BEFORE any User-agent line. Under RFC 9309 s.2.2.1 rules must be grouped under one or more user-agent lines, so rules preceding any User-agent are not part of any group and are discarded by conformant parsers (Google's parser behaves this way). On that reading the only valid group is 'User-agent: *' followed by 'Disallow:' with an empty value, which under RFC 9309 means allow everything. (b) Even if a lawyer insists on reading the orphaned block as expressing ASCI's intent, neither of the paths this tracker fetches appears in it. '/' is not listed. '/advisories/' is not listed. The nearest-looking entry, 'Disallow: /advice-resource/', does not prefix-match '/advisories/' and is a different WordPress custom-post-type archive. Both readings therefore yield: nothing we fetch is disallowed. POSITIVE SIGNAL: /advisories/ and / both carry <meta name='robots' content='index, follow, max-image-preview:large, max-snippet:-1, max-video-preview:-1'>, an affirmative machine-readable invitation to index. No X-Robots-Tag header on /advisories/. KEYWORD SWEEP: I ran a regex sweep for scrap/crawl/spider/robot/harvest/data mining/systematic/bulk/automated access/bots/text and data mining across all 27 documents fetched in this survey, with a positive control ('copyright') confirming the sweep was actually reading file contents. Zero hits on any host. OPERATOR: ASCI is NOT a government body and must not be treated as one. Its own About Us page states "ASCI was formed in 1985 by professionals from the advertising and media industry to keep Indian ads decent, fair and honest" — a voluntary, industry-funded self-regulatory organisation (registered non-profit, Mumbai). Its advisories are private publications, not public records, and none of the GoI free-reproduction conventions apply. RISK JUSTIFICATION — why medium rather than low, when the technical position is actually the cleanest of the four: robots.txt affirmatively allows our paths, the page carries index/follow, and there is no scraping clause. The elevation is not about access, it is about content rights. ASCI is the one private operator in this set; it grants no reuse licence and reserves all rights; and unlike the Gazette and TDSAT orders, ASCI advisories attract no public-record or judicial statutory exception under s.52 of the Copyright Act. So the metadata-only discipline is doing real legal work here rather than being a nicety. PRACTICAL GUIDANCE FOR COUNSEL: (1) storing title/date/type/link is low exposure — those are facts and short titles, not protected expression; (2) the optional PDF archive is the real exposure point, defensible as internal private reference but not as anything the firm circulates or republishes; (3) do not let ASCI advisory text or substantive extracts reach any client-facing or public output without permission; (4) the terms position could change without notice, since ASCI is a private site whose only terms document is an unfinished draft — worth re-checking periodically rather than treating this survey as durable.

opinion.bottom_line: Continue the tracker on 15 of the 17 hosts, but suspend two today: uidai.gov.in, whose robots.txt is a site-wide "User-Agent: * / Disallow: /" that covers both paths we fetch, and eservices.dot.gov.in, whose User Agreement names "web scraping" as the first example of an "unauthorised activity" and purports to bind by deemed consent on access. Everywhere else there is no robots rule covering our paths and no clause anywhere restricting automated access — the residual exposure is not access but reproduction, and it lands almost entirely on the optional PDF archive rather than the metadata dashboard, which stores bibliographic facts that attract no copyright. That archive position is materially stronger than it was six weeks ago: in ANI Media v. OpenAI (Delhi HC, 24 July 2026) Bansal J held prima facie that s.52(1)(a) carries no non-commercial limitation, that "private" extends to a closed corporate group, and expressly approved CCH Canadian's holding that lawyers researching to advise clients for profit are doing "research" — which is precisely this use case.

legal_basis.provision: Copyright Act 1957, s.2(k) read with s.17(d) and s.28
legal_basis.effect: Displaces the common instinct that government material is free. s.2(k) defines a "Government work" as one made or published by or under the direction or control of (i) the Government or any department, (ii) any Legislature in India, (iii) any Court, Tribunal or other judicial authority in India. s.17(d) vests first ownership in the Government absent agreement to the contrary, and s.28 runs the term for 60 years from the year following first publication. Consequence: copyright subsists in essentially everything the tracker touches on the 16 government hosts. The permissive website policies (MeitY, PIB, IN-SPACe, DoT) are therefore licences granted by the owner, and the restrictive ones (TEC /copyright-policy and /legal-disclaimer, MIB, CBFC, PRGI /website-policy) are genuine exercises of ownership, not boilerplate to be read past. ASCI is not a Government work at all.

legal_basis.provision: Copyright Act 1957, ss.13 and 14, and Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak (2008) 1 SCC 1
legal_basis.effect: The single most important provision for this tracker, and the reason the metadata dashboard is close to unassailable. Copyright subsists only in original works; the Supreme Court in EBC v. Modak rejected "sweat of the brow" and adopted a skill-and-judgment / modicum-of-creativity standard, holding that raw judicial text attracted no copyright in the publisher while copy-editing inputs did. Document titles, issue dates, document type and URL are facts and short titles, not protected expression, and their capture reproduces no substantial part of any work under s.14(a)(i). India also has no sui generis database right (unlike the EU), so a complainant must plead copyright in an original compilation, not mere investment in the collection.

Permits reproduction or publication of "any matter which has been published in any Official Gazette except an Act of a Legislature". This squarely covers egazette.gov.in, and covers TRAI regulations and directions and CERT-In s.70B directions TO THE EXTENT it is the gazette-notified instrument being copied. It must not be overclaimed: it attaches to the matter published in the Gazette, not to a regulator's website. It does not reach website HTML, navigation, editorial summaries, press releases, FAQs, consultation papers, guidance notes, or a PDF that only ever appeared on the site and was never carried in the Gazette. Application is document-by-document, not host-by-host.

A trap that cuts against the firm. An Act of a Legislature is permitted "subject to the condition that such Act is reproduced or published together with any commentary thereon or any other original matter". Bare archiving of a clean PDF of an Act — which is exactly what the tracker would do from mib.gov.in/en/documents/notification/acts-policy-guidelines or tec.gov.in — falls outside (q)(ii) because it carries no commentary, and outside (q)(i) because Acts are expressly excepted from it. Bare statutes are the weakest, not the strongest, category in the archive.

Narrower than commonly assumed and of limited use here. On the text it covers the report of a committee, commission, council, board or other like body "appointed by the Legislature", unless publication is prohibited by the Government. Reports of bodies appointed by a Ministry or a regulator — the great majority of what these hosts publish — are not obviously within it. Do not rely on this limb without checking the constituting instrument of the particular body.

Permits reproduction of "any judgment or order of a court, Tribunal or other judicial authority, unless the reproduction or publication of such judgment or order is prohibited by" that authority. It covers TDSAT judgments and orders, and TDSAT has published no prohibition — the survey confirmed the intended Copyright Policy page is commented out of the site and 404s at every path. But note precisely what the tracker actually fetches at TDSAT: /writereaddata/Delhi/docs/notices.php, a NOTICES listing. Notices, cause lists and administrative circulars are not judgments or orders, so (q)(iv) does not automatically cover the material being collected. Equally, a CBFC certification order is an administrative order of a statutory board, not of a judicial authority, so (q)(iv) does not reach cbfcindia.gov.in at all.

legal_basis.provision: Copyright Act 1957, s.52(1)(a)(i) and the Explanation to s.52(1)(a)
legal_basis.effect: The operative safe harbour for the PDF archive. Fair dealing with any work (not a computer programme) for the purposes of "private or personal use, including research" is not infringement, and the Explanation added in 2012 provides that "[t]he storing of any work in any electronic medium for the purposes mentioned in this clause ... shall not constitute infringement of copyright". So electronic storage for research is expressly within the exception rather than merely arguably so. Two conditions must both hold: a qualifying purpose (purpose test) and fairness (fairness test).

legal_basis.provision: ANI Media Pvt. Ltd. v. Open AI OpCo LLC, CS(COMM) 1028/2024, Delhi High Court (Bansal J), judgment 24 July 2026 — interim, prima facie
legal_basis.effect: Decided one month ago and directly on point; it substantially de-risks the archive. Held: (a) at paras 176-179, non-commercial use cannot be read into s.52(1)(a) — the legislature expressly confined other limbs (ss.52(1)(ad), (k)(ii), (l), (n), (o)) to non-commercial use and "[t]he requirement of non-commercial use is conspicuously absent in Section 52(1)(a)"; (b) at para 180 the Court expressly approved CCH Canadian, quoting with emphasis that "[r]esearch for the purpose of advising clients, giving opinions, arguing cases, preparing briefs and factums is nonetheless research. Lawyers carrying on the business of law for profit are conducting research"; (c) at para 208, "private" is not confined to individuals and "would include other private entities, including private companies", and at para 211 storage "in a closed space without access to the public" is "purely private"; (d) at paras 200-201, copies taken from material freely available on a website, without breaking a paywall or using unauthorised sources, are not infringing copies. Para 256 found both the purpose and fairness tests satisfied. CRUCIAL LIMITS: this is an interim order refusing an injunction, expressly prima facie, and para 274 records that the observations "would have no bearing on the final outcome of the suit". It is a first-instance interim ruling, appealable and liable to be revisited at trial. It is strong persuasive support, not a settled proposition.

Partial help only, and should not be over-relied on. (b) covers transient or incidental storage purely in the technical process of electronic transmission; (c) covers transient or incidental storage for the purpose of providing electronic links, access or integration where not expressly prohibited by the rights holder, subject to a 21-day takedown mechanism on written complaint. These support the link-and-metadata dashboard comfortably. They do not support a persistent PDF archive, which is neither transient nor incidental. Note also that (c) is disapplied where linking has been "expressly prohibited" — relevant to MTCTE, which requires prior TEC permission even for deep linking.

legal_basis.provision: Absence of any text-and-data-mining exception in Indian law
legal_basis.effect: Stated because a TMT partner will look for it. Unlike the EU (DSM Directive arts 3-4), Singapore (Copyright Act 2021 s.244) or Japan (art.30-4), s.52 contains no TDM or computational-analysis carve-out. The firm cannot rely on a mining exception; it must stand on the website licences, s.52(1)(q) where the document qualifies, or s.52(1)(a) as construed in ANI v. OpenAI.

legal_basis.provision: Copyright Act 1957, s.51 and s.63; M/s Knit Pro International v. State of NCT of Delhi (Supreme Court, 20 May 2022)
legal_basis.effect: Sets the ceiling on why archive discipline matters. s.51 defines infringement; s.63 makes knowing infringement an offence punishable with up to three years, and in Knit Pro the Supreme Court held that offence is cognizable and non-bailable. The threshold is "knowingly infringes", which an internal, unpublished archive supported by a documented licence-and-exception position does not plausibly meet — but the criminal characterisation is the reason not to let the archive drift outward without permissions in hand.

Civil liability, by way of compensation with no statutory cap since the 2008 amendment, where a person "without permission of the owner or any other person who is in charge of" a computer resource accesses it or downloads, copies or extracts data from it. Adjudication lies to an Adjudicating Officer under s.46 up to Rs.5 crore. This is the provision any complaint about the fetching itself would be built on, and the whole question turns on "without permission". GENUINELY UNSETTLED: there is no binding Indian appellate authority on whether requesting a page that the owner serves openly at HTTP 200, with no authentication, paywall or access control, is "without permission". The strong argument is that publication to the open internet carries implied permission to retrieve, reinforced here by RTI Act s.4 duties and by the sites' own hyperlinking policies inviting deep linking. ANI v. OpenAI did not decide the point — scraping-as-unauthorised-access was not pleaded in the interim application. The practical significance of an express exclusion (UIDAI's robots.txt, DoT's terms) is that it removes the implied-permission argument and supplies the "without permission" element that would otherwise be missing.

Criminalises doing any act referred to in s.43 "dishonestly or fraudulently" (those words carrying their IPC ss.24-25 meanings, now BNS 2023 ss.2(7) and 2(9)), with up to three years or Rs.5 lakh or both. The mental element is the whole defence: an openly identified crawler, running at about one request per second, honouring robots.txt, bypassing nothing, storing metadata for internal legal research and keeping a documented compliance file, is a poor candidate for dishonesty or fraud. This is precisely why the two operational changes below — honouring robots.txt as a hard gate, and dropping the spoofed Chrome User-Agent — do real legal work rather than being hygiene.

legal_basis.provision: Indian Contract Act 1872 ss.2, 7, 10 and 13-14, with IT Act 2000 s.10A
legal_basis.effect: Governs whether a website's browsewrap terms bind the firm at all. s.10A confirms that a contract is not unenforceable merely because it was formed electronically, but it does not manufacture assent: there must still be a proposal, communication, and acceptance that is absolute and unqualified, given with free consent. GENUINELY UNSETTLED: Indian courts have not definitively ruled on browsewrap enforceability. The discernible approach follows actual or constructive notice plus conduct evidencing assent, which is why clickwrap is routinely enforced and browsewrap is not. A footer link never navigated to by an automated client is a weak foundation. DoT's clause is the strongest of the set because it attempts to construct assent expressly ("By accessing Telecom eServices Portal it is deemed that you have given your consent"), but deeming language cannot by itself supply consent the Contract Act requires. Standard-form and unconscionability doctrine (Central Inland Water Transport v. Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986) 3 SCC 156; LIC v. Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995) 5 SCC 482) gives further room to resist an oppressive term in a non-negotiated instrument. This is an arguable position, not a clean answer, and it should be recorded as a considered position rather than assumed.

legal_basis.provision: robots.txt and RFC 9309 — evidential status, not legal status
legal_basis.effect: robots.txt is not law in India. No statute, rule or regulation gives it force; RFC 9309 is an IETF standard; non-compliance is not per se an offence or a tort. But it is not legally irrelevant either, and three effects matter. First, it is the operator's published, machine-readable statement of the scope of permission, so an express "Disallow: /" is the cleanest available rebuttal of the implied-permission argument that is the firm's primary answer to s.43 — it converts a dispute about silence into a dispute against an express statement. Second, it is contemporaneous documentary evidence of both the operator's position and the firm's knowledge of it (electronic records proved under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023, s.63), and knowledge of exclusion is what would supply the mental element under s.66; conversely, documented compliance is strong evidence of good faith. Third, it is the industry benchmark of reasonableness, relevant to relief, to quantum, and — most practically — to whether a regulator complains at all. Note the converse also appeared in ANI v. OpenAI, where intervenors argued that a rightsholder who "has chosen not to engage 'paywalls' or 'crawler blockers'" is poorly placed to complain. Two limits: robots governs ACCESS, not REUSE, so an "Allow" licenses no copying; and it is scoped per origin, so uidai.gov.in's exclusion does not as a matter of protocol bind backend.uidai.gov.in.

legal_basis.provision: Right to Information Act 2005, s.4(1)(b) and s.4(2)
legal_basis.effect: Supporting context rather than a licence. Public authorities are under a statutory duty of proactive disclosure and to provide as much information suo motu as possible, including through the internet, so the public need minimum resort to formal requests. This does not create a right in the firm to copy, but it strongly colours the reasonableness analysis: the tracker is collecting material these bodies are obliged to disseminate, in the manner they chose to disseminate it, which weighs against both a s.43 complaint and any suggestion of unfairness under s.52(1)(a).

legal_basis.provision: Government Open Data License – India (GODL-India), under NDSAP 2012
legal_basis.effect: Considered and found NOT to apply — stated so the firm does not lean on it. GODL grants a worldwide, royalty-free, non-exclusive licence to use, adapt, publish and create derivatives for lawful commercial and non-commercial purposes, conditioned on publishing an attribution statement identifying provider, source and licence with the DOI/URL/URI, and excluding personal information, sensitive data, logos and crests. But it attaches to datasets published under NDSAP on data.gov.in and to resources that expressly adopt it. Not one of the 17 surveyed hosts mentions GODL. It is therefore relevant only in two ways: as evidence that the Government of India's own default open-data posture is permissive-with-attribution, which is context for reading the restrictive outliers; and as an alternative lawful route if any of the same documents are mirrored on data.gov.in, where GODL would apply on its own terms.

legal_basis.provision: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, s.3(c)(ii)
legal_basis.effect: Secondary but worth managing. The Act does not apply to personal data made publicly available by the Data Principal, or by a person under a legal obligation under Indian law to make it publicly available. Documents published by these authorities under RTI s.4 or their own statutory publication duties fall within limb (B). The exemption is not a general "it was on the internet" carve-out, and it is assessed against the particular data. Practical effect: the metadata dashboard is unaffected, but a growing PDF archive containing, say, PRGI registration particulars or CBFC or TDSAT filings should not be turned into a person-searchable index, which would be a different processing purpose from the one the exemption comfortably covers.

Named because it will be asked about, and to record that it is not engaged. s.38 creates offences around unauthorised access to the Central Identities Data Repository. The tracker touches only UIDAI's public website, not the CIDR, so s.38 is not in play. s.47 additionally bars cognizance of Aadhaar Act offences except on a complaint by the Authority or an officer it authorises. The UIDAI exposure is the robots exclusion under the IT Act and the commercial carve-out in its Copyright Policy, not the Aadhaar Act.

per_host_risk.why: robots.txt disallows only Drupal internals, admin, auth, /search/ and oembed — none of our three paths; no automated-access clause anywhere in its policies; deep linking expressly needs no permission. Only condition is a non-standard Copyright Policy requiring prior email permission to reproduce, which bites the PDF archive, not metadata. Express no-framing rule.

Its /terms-use defines "Unauthorised activities" to include "web scraping" by name as the first example, makes it operative via "shall not in any manner be used for any unauthorized activity", separately confines access to "interfaces expressly authorised by DoT", binds by deemed consent on access, and threatens "Criminal/ Civil action". Robots is permissive (403 = unavailable = access allowed under RFC 9309) and the Copyright Policy is the fully permissive GoI clause — but the copyright grant licenses reuse and does not cure a restriction on the METHOD of collection.

No robots.txt, and a keyword sweep of both policy pages found no clause on robots, crawling, scraping or systematic downloading. The permission-to-reproduce condition is contradicted twice on the operator's own site — including both versions on the same page — which materially weakens any argument that a clear condition was accepted. Operational: HEAD returns 401 with no WWW-Authenticate; the tracker must use GET.

robots.txt is "User-agent: * / Disallow:" — the idiom for allow-everything, so crawling is affirmatively permitted and no rule matches. The exposure is reproduction: three mutually contradictory copyright statements, two of them restrictive, and /legal-disclaimer expressly forecloses the implied-licence argument ("Your access to it does not imply a license to reproduce and/or distribute this information"). Metadata-only is safe; the PDF archive is not.

No robots.txt and no automated-access clause; /get_er_list is a public unauthenticated JSON endpoint of largely uncopyrightable fact (equipment names, certificate numbers, dates). Elevated because the Copyright Policy was deliberately amended to require prior email permission with no competing permissive clause on this host, deep linking itself is said to require prior TEC permission, and framing is expressly prohibited. Operational: HEAD returns 403, GET returns 200 — use GET; never touch /login or its CAPTCHA.

robots.txt is "User-agent: * / Allow: /"; the "Terms of use" page is a pure disclaimer creating no use conditions; the Copyright Policy is the fully permissive GoI clause allowing reproduction in any format without specific permission; deep linking expressly permitted. A 50-page sweep of the CMS found no automated-access clause. The tracker uses the site's own published REST endpoint. Only residual: documents marked as third-party copyright fall outside the grant.

No robots.txt (the 200 is a soft 404 — proven by an identical 938-byte response to a bogus control path), no automated-access clause across eleven policy pages, and deep linking expressly permitted, so access is unobjectionable. Elevated solely because reproduction is conditioned on "taking proper permission by sending a mail to us" first, which the PDF archive engages on the clause's plain words. Operational: this host answers 200 for every URL, so validate Content-Type and body or it will ingest error pages as documents.

The only host in the survey whose robots.txt actually covers the paths we fetch. The complete file is "User-Agent: * / Disallow: /" — a site-wide exclusion of every agent, with no Allow rule to override it, confirmed not to be UA-conditional. Both /en/circulars and /en/gazetted-notifications are squarely within it. Compounded by a Copyright Policy that, uniquely in this survey, confines reproduction of extracts to "research or private study but not for sale or for use in conjunction with commercial purposes" — a clause aimed at exactly a commercial law firm.

per_host_risk.risk: medium doctrinally — treat as high operationally
per_host_risk.why: No robots.txt on this origin, and robots is scoped per origin under RFC 9309, so the parent's "Disallow: /" does not bind it and no rule is breached. But this is the asset backend of the one operator that has excluded all crawlers site-wide, and it is where whole-document PDF copying actually happens — relying on the per-origin technicality is relying on a configuration gap, and it should not be treated differently from its parent. Also correct the path inventory: /en/circulars 404s here; the real prefix is /get/files/.

The most permissive host in the survey: no Terms of Use exists at all (the footer links to one, and the Privacy Policy cross-refers to one, but none is published), no automated-access clause, and a Copyright Policy granting reproduction "free of charge in any format or media without requiring specific permission" with no commercial carve-out — broader than UIDAI's and sufficient for both dashboard and archive. robots.txt is a broken allowlist (about 30 Allow lines with no "Disallow: /"), so it restricts nothing but the password-reset endpoint; our /api/now/sp/page is not among the enumerated pages, so prefer the documented /inspace?id=... URLs to align with evident intent.

robots.txt is 403, i.e. unavailable, which under RFC 9309 permits access, and the 403 is not bot-targeted. Elevated for reproduction: the Copyright Policy is the restrictive variant requiring prior permission and self-declares that no third-party content is used, removing that carve-out. Two live operational facts: a hidden fp/fingerprint.html bot-fingerprinting iframe, and observed intermittent connection drops under rapid sequential requests. UNVERIFIED: the separate "Terms & Condition" tab is AJAX-loaded and could not be retrieved, so it is not established that this host lacks an automated-access clause.

Stock Drupal robots.txt served at 200; every Disallow targets Drupal internals, admin, auth, oembed and /search/ — none is a document-listing path. Deep linking expressly requires no prior permission, and /terms-conditions grants free-of-charge reproduction subject to accuracy and acknowledgement; the conflicting restrictive Copyright Policy on /website-policy is the only wrinkle and bears on the archive. LIVE RULE TO RESPECT: Disallow: /search/ — do not harvest via the search endpoint. Path inventory is wrong: the two supplied paths are MIB paths and 404 here.

No robots.txt, so nothing to breach on access, and the orders page serves cleanly to an anonymous GET. Elevated because the Copyright Policy is squarely restrictive, has no third-party carve-out, and is backed by an all-rights-reserved footer — the PDF archive is straightforward copying without the permission the clause requires. Also sits behind an F5 BIG-IP ASM that actively rejected /sitemap.xml with a support-ID block page; a block must be a stop-and-alert condition, never a retry loop.

No robots.txt, no terms in existence (the sole footer policy link, Disclaimer.aspx, renders only a pagenotfound placeholder — verified twice, including inside a live ASP.NET session), and no scraping clause. The About Us page is internally contradictory, asserting Controller of Publications copyright alongside a statement that the Gazette is "available in the public domain". That tension is immaterial here because this is the one host where s.52(1)(q)(i) squarely applies: its content is by definition matter published in an Official Gazette.

The strongest position in the survey. robots.txt is a soft 404 that parses to an empty ruleset, i.e. allow-all under either reading; the Terms and Conditions are purely an accuracy disclaimer and liability cap imposing no restriction on access method or volume; and the Copyright Policy affirmatively grants reproduction "free of charge and there is no need for any prior approval". Both metadata and archive sit inside that grant. Two conditions: prominent acknowledgement if output is ever issued to others, and the third-party-material carve-out, which matters because PIB releases often embed other departments' material.

There is simply nothing to breach: no robots.txt, no terms restricting access, no scraping clause, and no copyright policy at all — the intended Copyright Policy is commented out of the Website Policies page and 404s at all nine probed paths, so no prohibition on reproduction exists for s.52(1)(q)(iv) purposes. The site is silent rather than permissive, so there is no express licence to lean on. Note the precision point: the tracker fetches the NOTICES listing, which is administrative material, not judgments or orders, so s.52(1)(q)(iv) does not automatically cover what is actually being collected.

The only private operator, and it must not be treated as a government site. Access is the cleanest in the survey — robots.txt allows our paths under both readings of a malformed file, and /advisories/ carries an affirmative <meta name='robots' content='index, follow'>. The elevation is entirely about content rights: ASCI grants no reuse licence, reserves all rights, and, being neither a government body nor a judicial authority, offers no route into any limb of s.52(1)(q). Metadata-only discipline is doing real legal work here rather than being a nicety. Its only terms document is an unfinished draft still carrying editorial markers, so the position could change without notice.

obligations: Honour robots.txt as a hard pre-flight gate, fetched per origin at the start of every run and evaluated under RFC 9309, with the run aborting for any host whose rules cover the target path. This is not legally mandatory in India, but it is the single cheapest step that preserves the implied-permission argument under IT Act s.43 and negates the dishonesty element under s.66.

Stop automated collection from uidai.gov.in immediately, and from backend.uidai.gov.in with it. Also stop eservices.dot.gov.in, or obtain DoT's written authorisation first. Lawyer-initiated manual browsing of all three remains unaffected.

Replace the spoofed Chrome User-Agent with an identifying string naming the firm and a contact mailbox (e.g. "LRLabs-RegTracker/1.0 (+mailto:webmaster@<firm>.in)"). Presenting a browser UA while running unattended is the fact pattern that makes a technical breach look like circumvention; an honest UA is evidence of good faith and gives an operator someone to email instead of someone to complain about.

Rate limiting and load discipline: keep to at most one request per second per host, serial rather than parallel, cap runs per day, use exponential backoff on 429s, 5xx and connection resets, and treat a WAF block page as a stop-and-alert condition rather than a retry trigger — specifically the F5 ASM block on cbfcindia.gov.in and the intermittent drops on mib.gov.in.

Use GET, never HEAD, on nccs.gov.in and www.mtcte.tec.gov.in. Both return 401/403 to HEAD with no WWW-Authenticate header while serving anonymous GET at 200; this is method-level rejection, not an access control, and the distinction should be documented so that no one later characterises the tracker as having worked around a control.

Validate Content-Type and body content before ingesting, never status codes alone. www.cert-in.org.in returns HTTP 200 for every URL including missing ones, pib.gov.in and egazette.gov.in serve soft 404s, and www.inspace.gov.in returns 200 ServiceNow login stubs at conventional policy paths. Without this the archive will silently fill with error pages presented as documents.

Do not harvest via prgi.gov.in/search/ — it is a live Disallow rule in a robots.txt that is otherwise permissive as to our paths, and it is the one operative crawl restriction the firm must actually code around.

Never render any of these hosts inside an iframe. TRAI, MTCTE, MeitY, CERT-In, UIDAI, IN-SPACe and PRGI all expressly prohibit framing ("we do not permit our pages to be loaded into frames on your site"), and eservices.dot.gov.in enforces it technically via a content-security-policy: frame-ancestors 'self' header. The dashboard must link out, opening in a new window.

Carry attribution on every stored item and on any internal extract, in the form: "Source: <issuing body>, <document title>, <date>. Retrieved from <full URL> on <date>. Reproduced from the official website of <body>." For UIDAI material the Copyright Policy requires acknowledgement "citing the uniform resource locator (URL) of the article/page", so the URL is mandatory, not optional. Attribution is a condition of the permissive licences (MeitY, PIB, IN-SPACe, DoT, PRGI /terms-conditions) and mitigation under the restrictive ones.

Never present tracked text as authoritative. Almost every host disclaims that its content "should not be construed as a statement of law or used for any legal purposes", and TEC, NCCS and MTCTE state that where the website differs from the Act or Rules, the latter prevails. The dashboard must carry a standing banner to that effect, and no tracked item may be cited in advice without verification against the e-Gazette or the issuing body's authoritative text.

Keep the PDF archive strictly internal: access-controlled to the firm's own personnel, no circulation to clients, no external distribution, no inclusion in outward-facing work product without separate permission. Its entire defensibility rests on being a closed, unpublished, internal store — which is precisely the "closed space without access to the public" characterisation the Delhi High Court accepted at para 211 of ANI v. OpenAI.

Make PDF archiving a per-host flag, defaulting OFF for every host whose reproduction terms are restrictive or require prior permission: TRAI, CERT-In, TEC, MTCTE, MIB, CBFC, ASCI, and both UIDAI hosts. Default ON is defensible only for MeitY, PIB, IN-SPACe, e-Gazette, TDSAT, PRGI and NCCS.

Flag and exclude from archiving any document explicitly marked as third-party copyright. Every permissive policy in the survey carves this out, and PIB releases in particular frequently embed other departments' material to which PIB's permission does not extend.

Retain request logs with timestamps, target URLs, response codes and per-run request counts. If the firm is ever challenged, the ability to evidence roughly 53 requests per run at one per second is the proportionality defence — and under s.43 it is also the answer to any suggestion of disruption or impairment.

Keep the archive within DPDP Act s.3(c)(ii): do not build a person-searchable index over archived documents, and set a retention and review cycle. The exemption covers data an authority is obliged to publish, not any downstream repurposing the firm chooses to build on top of it.

Record the firm's considered legal position in a dated file note — implied permission for openly served pages, browsewrap non-assent, s.52(1)(q) where applicable, s.52(1)(a) as construed in ANI v. OpenAI. Having turned its mind to the question contemporaneously is directly relevant to the mental element under IT Act s.66 and to quantum in any s.46 adjudication.
red_flags: uidai.gov.in — GENUINELY PROHIBITIVE ON ACCESS. Its robots.txt, in full, is "User-Agent: *" followed by "Disallow: /". That is the strongest exclusion the protocol can express, it applies to every agent including ours, there is no Allow rule to override it, and it was confirmed not to vary by User-Agent. Both paths the tracker fetches — /en/circulars and /en/gazetted-notifications — are squarely within it. This is the only host in the survey where a robots rule actually covers what we fetch. Sending a Chrome User-Agent does not take the tracker outside the rule; it makes the position worse by making unattended collection look like circumvention.

eservices.dot.gov.in — GENUINELY PROHIBITIVE ON TERMS. Its User Agreement at /terms-use defines "Unauthorised activities" to include "any activity which is punishable under section 43 (for eg web scraping, altering source code, hacking, introducing viruses etc.)", makes that operative through "Telecom eServices Portal shall not in any manner be used for any unauthorized activity", separately requires that services "be accessed only through the interfaces expressly authorised by DoT", deems consent on access, and warns that contravention will be "viewed strictly and appropriate Criminal/ Civil action will be initiated". It names the exact activity, on the exact host. It is not volume-qualified, harm-qualified, or limited to commercial reuse, so none of the tracker's proportionality facts take it outside the clause's literal words. Do not read the permissive Copyright Policy on the same host as curing this — that clause licenses reuse, this one restricts the method of collection.

backend.uidai.gov.in — the firm would be relying on a configuration gap. There is no robots.txt on this origin and robots is scoped per origin, so as a matter of protocol nothing is breached. But this is the asset backend of the one operator that has excluded all crawlers site-wide, and it is where the PDF archive actually pulls whole documents from. The protocol point is sound; the optics are poor, and the firm should know that is what it is standing on rather than believing it has permission.

UIDAI's Copyright Policy contains the only clause in the survey that expressly reaches a commercial law firm: extracts may be reproduced "for research or private study but not for sale or for use in conjunction with commercial purposes". A private internal archive is not "for sale", but "use in conjunction with commercial purposes" is broad enough to reach it. ANI v. OpenAI helps on the statutory exception but does not override an express contractual/licence limitation the firm is on notice of.

Restrictive or prior-permission reproduction clauses on eight hosts, all of which bite the optional PDF archive and none of which bites the metadata dashboard: TRAI, CERT-In and MTCTE each require prior permission "by sending a mail"; www.tec.gov.in carries two restrictive statements including a legal disclaimer that expressly negates any implied licence to reproduce; MIB and CBFC use the flat "may not be reproduced ... without due permission" variant; and PRGI's /website-policy contradicts its own permissive /terms-conditions. Each is curable by one email.

www.ascionline.in is a private self-regulatory body, not a government one. It grants no reuse licence, its only copyright statement is "All Rights Reserved", and no limb of s.52(1)(q) is available to it — no Gazette, no Act, no judgment or order. Its advisories are private publications. This is the one host where losing metadata-only discipline would create real, unmitigated copyright exposure.

The tracker currently sends a spoofed Chrome User-Agent. On the 15 permissive hosts this is merely poor practice; on any host that has expressed non-consent it converts an arguable technical breach into an evidential problem, because it is indistinguishable from deliberate concealment. Fix this before the next run regardless of which hosts are retained.

Anti-framing prohibitions on seven hosts (TRAI, MTCTE, MeitY, CERT-In, UIDAI, IN-SPACe, PRGI), plus a technically enforced frame-ancestors policy on DoT. These are express, unambiguous and currently unbreached — but they would be breached the moment the dashboard embeds a source page rather than linking out. MTCTE additionally exposes an ?embed=true parameter that strips navigation; using it to frame content would run directly into the prohibition.

UNVERIFIED, and therefore a flag rather than a finding: mib.gov.in's separate "Terms & Condition" tab could not be retrieved (AJAX endpoints returned empty shells and a 500, and every standalone path 404s). It is not established that this host lacks an automated-access clause. Treat MIB's clean scraping position as provisional until that tab is read.

Path inventory errors that must be corrected before any of this analysis can be relied on host-by-host: the two paths attributed to prgi.gov.in are in fact MIB paths and 404 on PRGI; /en/circulars 404s on backend.uidai.gov.in, whose real content sits under /get/files/; and RssMain.aspx is a PIB path that was being requested against egazette.gov.in and tdsat.gov.in, where it returns 500 and 404 respectively.

A precision point that cuts against an assumption the firm may be making: s.52(1)(q)(iv) covers judgments and orders, but the TDSAT path actually fetched is a NOTICES listing, which is administrative rather than judicial material. Likewise a CBFC order is an administrative order of a statutory board, not of a judicial authority. Neither is automatically within (q)(iv). And bare PDFs of Acts fall outside both (q)(i), which excepts Acts, and (q)(ii), which requires accompanying commentary.

caveats: This is a compliance review of publicly stated terms as observed on 25 August 2026, not a legal opinion. It has not been settled by counsel, no duty of care is assumed, and it should be adopted as the firm's own advice before being relied on externally. Several conclusions turn on arguable positions rather than settled law and are identified as such.

Website terms change without notice and several of these hosts are demonstrably unstable. www.tec.gov.in renders "Last reviewed and updated on" with today's date, which appears to be dynamically generated and cannot be relied on as a genuine review date; CERT-In's footer does the same. TRAI's Copyright Policy shows a last update of 24 August 2026 — one day before this survey. Any conclusion here has a short shelf life.

One material gap: mib.gov.in's separate "Terms & Condition" tab could not be retrieved. The four AJAX-loaded policy tabs returned empty shells or HTTP 500, and every standalone path 404s. The finding that MIB has no automated-access clause is therefore provisional and covers only the pages that could actually be read.

The survey did not classify documents individually against s.52(1)(q). Whether a given instrument is matter published in an Official Gazette, an Act, a report of a body appointed by the Legislature, or a judgment or order is a document-by-document question, and the exception applies or fails at that level rather than at host level. The generalisations here are directional, not determinative for any particular PDF.

The reliance on ANI Media v. OpenAI is reliance on an interim, prima facie ruling of a single judge refusing an injunction, which expressly records at para 274 that its observations "would have no bearing on the final outcome of the suit". It is appealable and revisitable at trial. It is the best and most recent Indian authority on s.52(1)(a) and commercial research, and it was not decided on facts identical to these — it concerned LLM training storage, not a document archive, and scraping-as-unauthorised-access, robots.txt and website terms were not pleaded or decided in it.

Two questions of Indian law engaged here are genuinely unsettled and no clean answer should be reported upward: whether fetching a page served openly at HTTP 200 without authentication is "without permission of the owner" for IT Act s.43, on which there is no binding appellate authority; and whether browsewrap terms bind absent affirmative assent, on which Indian courts have not definitively ruled. The firm's positions on both are arguable and well-supported but not risk-free.

This survey covers only the 17 hosts listed and only the representative paths supplied. Some of those paths were wrong — the PRGI paths belong to MIB, backend.uidai.gov.in does not serve /en/circulars, and RssMain.aspx was attributed to two hosts it does not belong to — so per-host conclusions must be re-checked against the tracker's actual URL list before being relied on.

No review was conducted of the tracker's source code, its production request rate, the User-Agent actually sent in production, its retention behaviour, or its access controls. Every operational fact relied on here — one request per second, roughly 53 requests per run, metadata-only storage, internal-only dashboard, no authentication bypassed — is taken from the instructions given and has not been independently verified against the running system. If any of those is inaccurate, the analysis changes.

No assessment was made of: state-level or non-listed hosts; the firm's professional-conduct obligations under Bar Council of India rules; whether any output attracts privilege; contractual restrictions in the firm's own client engagements; or the position under any law other than those cited. The Aadhaar Act was considered only to record that the CIDR is not touched.

GODL-India was checked and does not apply — no surveyed host adopts it. If the firm later sources the same documents from data.gov.in, that material would come under GODL's own terms and would need separate attribution handling; that route has not been assessed here.

The DPDP analysis is a flag, not a conclusion. Whether particular archived documents contain personal data, and whether each falls within the s.3(c)(ii) exemption, was not examined document-by-document, and the phased commencement of the DPDP Rules should be confirmed against current notifications before any compliance position is finalised.

Absence of a restriction is not permission. On several hosts — TDSAT, IN-SPACe, e-Gazette, backend.uidai.gov.in — the finding is silence rather than a grant. Silence is not prohibition and supports the activity, but it gives the firm no licence to point to if the operator later publishes terms or objects, and it should not be recorded internally as though it were consent.
